title: Cognitive_computing
summary:
Cognitive computing refers to technology platforms that, broadly speaking, are based on the scientific disciplines of artificial intelligence and signal processing. These platforms encompass machine learning, reasoning, natural language processing, speech recognition and vision (object recognition), human-computer interaction, dialog and narrative generation, among other technologies.

At present, there is no widely agreed upon definition for cognitive computing in either academia or industry. In general, the term has been used to refer to new hardware and/or software that mimics the functioning of the human brain. Cognitive computing is a new type of computing with the goal of more accurate models of how the human brain senses, reasons, and responds to stimulus. Cognitive computing-branded technology platforms typically specialize in the processing and analysis of large, unstructured datasets.

While many cognitive systems employ techniques originating in artificial intelligence research, cognitive systems themselves may not be artificially intelligent. The term "cognitive system" applies to any artificial construct able to perform a cognitive process, where a cognitive process is the transformation of data, information, knowledge, or wisdom to a new level in the DIKW Pyramid.

In situations where humans work collaboratively with cognitive systems (called a human/cog ensemble), results achieved by the ensemble are superior to results obtainable by the human working alone, meaning the human is cognitively augmented. When the ensemble achieves results at or superior to the level of a human expert, it has achieved synthetic expertise. Applications include education (personalized learning assistants for students) and healthcare (identifying carcinogens and other diagnostic tasks). IBM developed Watson in 2013 and the TrueNorth neuromorphic chip in 2014, followed by the NorthPole chip in 2023 which achieved speeds about 4,000 times faster than TrueNorth.
